lesson.title: Same Destination, Same Energy: The Path Independence Trick
lesson.summary: Hess's law says the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same no matter how many steps you break it into, because enthalpy is a state function and energy cannot appear or disappear along the way.
lesson.body:
Imagine hiking to the top of a hill. Whether you walk straight up the steepest slope or take a long winding trail, your net change in altitude is identical: it depends only on where you started and where you ended, not on the path you took. Enthalpy behaves the same way. It is a state function, meaning its value depends only on the current condition of a system (temperature, pressure, composition), not on the history of how the system got there. Hess's law is the direct consequence of that fact applied to chemical reactions: the total enthalpy change for converting a set of reactants into a set of products is the same whether the reaction happens in one step or through any number of intermediate steps.

The deeper reason this must be true is energy conservation, the first law of thermodynamics. If two different reaction pathways between the same reactants and the same products released different amounts of net energy, you could in principle run the reaction forward along the cheap path and backward along the expensive path, extracting energy from nothing every cycle. That would violate conservation of energy, so nature simply does not allow it. Hess's law is really conservation of energy wearing chemistry clothes, and this is why it also licenses a set of algebraic moves: you can add thermochemical equations together and add their delta H values, you can reverse an equation as long as you flip the sign of delta H (running a reaction backward releases what forward absorbed, and vice versa), and you can multiply an equation by any factor as long as you multiply delta H by that same factor.

Here is a worked check of path independence using real thermochemical data. The direct formation of carbon dioxide from graphite is C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g), delta H = -393.5 kJ. Now consider a two-step alternate path to the same overall reaction. Step 1: C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO(g), delta H1 = -110.5 kJ. Step 2: CO(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO2(g), delta H2 = -283.0 kJ. Adding steps 1 and 2, the intermediate CO cancels (it is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2), and the two halves of O2 combine into one full O2, leaving the same overall equation, C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g). Adding the enthalpies: -110.5 kJ + (-283.0 kJ) = -393.5 kJ. That matches the direct, one-step value exactly. It genuinely does not matter whether carbon burns straight to CO2 or passes through CO along the way: the net energy released getting from graphite and oxygen gas to carbon dioxide is the same either way.

This might look like a neat coincidence the first time you see it, but it is guaranteed by the state-function property of enthalpy, and it connects directly back to why delta H of reaction is worth tabulating at all: once you accept that paths do not matter, a handful of measured or tabulated delta H values for simple reactions can be combined to predict the enthalpy of reactions that are difficult, dangerous, or practically impossible to run and measure directly. That predictive combination is the subject of the next chapter, Hess's law calculations, where you will manipulate given equations, reversing and scaling them as needed, so that they sum to a target reaction you actually care about.
